headline: Captree dock talk: the bunker got squeezed, and the bass finally showed up to eat
subhead: The new moon tide packed bait tight against the beach this week — here's where the bass and blues committed, and why the fluke bite keeps thinning out.
body_markdown:
Stood at the Captree dock Tuesday morning listening to a mate off one of the head boats tell anybody who'd listen that Democrat Point looked like a washing machine at first light — birds stacked, bunker getting pushed up on the sand, and something big underneath just leaning on them. That's the story of this week on the South Shore, and it's about time.

The new moon on the 10th put real muscle behind the tide, and that's exactly what this bay and this beach needed. Bunker schools that had been loafing around the inlet mouth and drifting along the surf line all August finally got squeezed — tight against the beach at Robert Moses, stacked in the wash off Democrat Point, and pinned up into the back bay creeks around Babylon and Sayville on the bigger push. Bass that had been picking at stragglers all summer started committing hard. We flagged this last week — said the blitz activity would build as the new moon tide tightened bait against the surf line, and that's exactly what's playing out now.

Offshore, the ocean's been a little unruly — buoys out past the inlet were reading close to 4-foot swell at a short 5-second period for stretches of the week, which is enough to keep the surf guys honest about footing but not enough to shut things down. Water temp out in open water is sitting around 71, still plenty warm, and there's a real gap between that open-ocean number and what's happening inside the inlet and back in the bay, where shallow flats and creek mouths are running warmer under the afternoon sun. That thermal split is doing exactly what it always does this time of year — it's pushing the productive water inside. The inlet channels, the flats off Nicoll Bay, the deeper cuts by the Robert Moses bridges — that's where the action's concentrated right now, not out on the open beach where the swell's knocking things around.

Bass fishing has been the story. Guys working bunker schools at Democrat Point and along the ocean side of Fire Island have been snagging bunker on weighted trebles and dropping them back on a fish-finder rig, and connecting with slot fish and a scattering of overslots mixed into the schools. If you don't want to snag-and-drop, a big white or bone-colored darter or a bunker-profile swimmer worked through the edges of a visible boil is getting hit too — the fish are committed enough right now that presentation matters less than being in the right piece of water at the right stage of the tide. Best window's been the last two hours of the incoming pushing into the top of the tide, right as the bait gets squeezed against the beach with nowhere left to go.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait, and they've been the more reliable bite for anybody who doesn't want to wait around for the bass to show. Poppers and bunker spoons worked over the same boils at Democrat Point and off the Robert Moses jetties have been drawing cocktail blues and the occasional bigger chopper. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks from Babylon through Patchogue — small stuff on tiny bucktails and spearing off the docks, but it's a good sign, because that first wave of snappers usually means the adult run isn't far behind as the water keeps cooling.

Fluke, on the other hand, are winding down, and it's not just a bad week — it's the calendar. The keeper-grade fish that were stacking up around the Robert Moses bridges and the deeper cuts of the bay through the summer have largely slid off toward cooler, deeper structure, which is the classic move this time of year. What's left inshore is mostly short fish. If you're still chasing them, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 20 to 30 feet off the bridge pilings on the outgoing tide, will still put fish in the boat — just don't expect a lot of keepers in the mix. Weakfish have been a nice surprise bycatch on the bay flats around high water, a few keeper-class fish coming on cut bunker fished on the bottom over grassy stretches off Nicoll Bay, but it's inconsistent enough that I wouldn't build a whole trip around it.

Looking ahead, the tide's still carrying plenty of push out of this new moon, and the bunker aren't going anywhere fast with bass and blues leaning on them this hard. Expect the inlet and beachfront blitz activity to hold, maybe build a touch more, over the next few days as bait stays squeezed and water keeps cooling. If the ocean lays down even a little, Democrat Point and the ocean side of Robert Moses are worth the early wake-up call — first light on the last of the incoming has been the stretch producing the most committed fish. If you can only get one day in this weekend, that's the window I'd plan around, with a plan B tucked into the bay in case the swell keeps things sloppy out front.
